data.name: Ticker_TimeJubileesFull
data.value: Since {baseDateName} on {baseDate:d}, incredible milestones of time have passed. The next big marker is {nextJubilee} on {nearestJubileeDate:d}!

data.name: Info_TimeJubileesMethod
data.value:
The word "Jubilee" traces back to the Hebrew yobel - the ram's horn trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement to open a sacred 50-year reset: slaves freed, debts cancelled, lands returned. That 50-year cycle became the model for all milestone anniversaries in Western culture.

Different civilisations layered in their own "round" numbers. The Romans celebrated the Decennalia (10 years) and Vicennalia (20 years) of an emperor's reign - Constantine the Great famously staged elaborate games for both. Medieval Christianity added the Silver (25th) and Golden (50th) jubilees. The Diamond jubilee concept (60th/75th) was coined in England during Queen Victoria's reign in 1897.

Why do round numbers feel so satisfying? Cognitive psychologists call it processing fluency - the brain rewards itself for recognising patterns that are easy to encode and recall. Numbers ending in 0 or 5, repeated digits (111, 33), and powers of 10 all trigger this reward because they compress cleanly into memory. Evolutionary pressure reinforced this: a hunter-gatherer who could quickly grasp "about 100 animals" had a survival advantage over one trying to count to 97.

This app identifies every such milestone in your personal timeline - both the classical jubilees and the mathematically satisfying ones your calendar never told you about.

data.name: Info_TimeJubileesSource
data.value: Detailed breakdown of the exact time units remaining until your next major life milestone based on proprietary base-10 mathematics.

data.name: Ticker_CountdownFull_WithDays

data.name: Info_CountdownMethod
data.value:
This ticker locks onto the nearest upcoming anniversary and runs a live countdown to it, refreshing every second.

The calculation takes the exact timestamp of the base date, advances it by the target number of days, and subtracts the current time to yield the remaining interval. The result is then decomposed into days, hours, minutes, and seconds using standard modular arithmetic.

Why does this feel meaningful? Research in motivational psychology shows that a visible countdown to a defined goal - even a symbolic one - increases goal salience and temporal awareness. Athletes, students, and project managers all perform better when a deadline is made concrete. We bring that same psychological sharpening to the milestones of your own life.

data.name: Info_CountdownSource
data.value: Detailed breakdown of the exact time units remaining until your next major life milestone based on proprietary base-10 mathematics.

data.name: Ticker_LifeOdometerFull
data.value: Approximately {heartbeats:N0} heartbeats have drummed and {breaths:N0} breaths have been processed since {baseDateName} on {baseDate:d}.

data.name: Info_LifeOdometerMethod
data.value:
Your body is running two clocks that never pause. The heart averages 60-100 beats per minute; the medical consensus reference value used here is 70 bpm, the widely-cited resting average for adults. Over a single day that is 100,800 beats; over a decade, roughly 3.68 billion.

The respiratory system cycles at 12-20 breaths per minute at rest. This ticker uses the NCBI reference of 16 breaths/min, yielding 23,040 breaths per day.

Both rates are population averages - individual values vary by age, fitness level, altitude, and stress, but the aggregate numbers remain strikingly large.

The "odometer" metaphor is deliberate: just as a car's odometer records distance regardless of speed, your biological odometer accumulates counts regardless of what you were doing - sleeping, laughing, or reading this screen. By the time you turn 80, your heart will have beaten approximately 2.98 billion times and your lungs will have completed roughly 672 million breath cycles.

data.name: Info_LifeOdometerSource
data.value: Calculation based on the data provided by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) of the National Library of Medicine (NIH).

data.name: Ticker_AlienAnniversariesFull
data.value: Since {baseDateName} on {baseDate:d}, the planets have finished their laps at different speeds. On Mars, this timeline has spanned {marsYears:F2} Martian years, while on Venus, this timeline has spanned {venusYears:F2} Venusian years.

data.name: Info_AlienAnniversariesMethod
data.value:
Every planet orbits the Sun at its own pace, governed by Kepler's Third Law: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Closer planets move faster; distant ones crawl.

Mars (687 Earth days / year): A Martian day - called a sol - is 24 hours, 39 minutes, 35 seconds, only 40 minutes longer than Earth's. NASA's rovers use sol-based mission clocks. Your age in Martian years is roughly half your Earth age.

Venus (225 Earth days / year, 243-day rotation): Venus is cosmically bizarre. It rotates so slowly - and backwards (retrograde) - that a single Venusian day is longer than a Venusian year. If you stood on Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east, crawling across the sky over 117 Earth days.

Jupiter (4,333 Earth days / year): A year on Jupiter lasts about 11.86 Earth years, yet Jupiter spins faster than any other planet - one Jovian day is only 10 hours. Its rapid rotation causes the planet to bulge visibly at the equator.

Saturn (10,759 Earth days / year): A Saturnian year spans 29.4 Earth years. For most people, Saturn has completed fewer than 3 full orbits since their birth.

These alien anniversaries are not just novelties - space agencies use planetary time to schedule mission windows, orbital insertions, and hibernation cycles for interplanetary spacecraft.

data.name: Info_AlienAnniversariesSource
data.value: Data courtesy of the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System.

data.name: Ticker_GalacticCommuteFull
data.value: Since {baseDate:d}, Earth has hitched a ride for a {distance} journey around the center of the Milky Way.

data.name: Ticker_GalacticCommuteFullWithRounded
data.value: Since {baseDate:d}, Earth has hitched a ride for a {distance} ({fullDistance}) journey around the center of the Milky Way.

data.name: Info_GalacticCommuteMethod
data.value:
The Solar System is not sitting still - it is hurtling around the centre of the Milky Way at roughly 220-230 km/s (about 514,000 mph, or 1/1,300th of the speed of light). One complete orbit is called a Galactic Year or Cosmic Year, and it takes approximately 225-230 million Earth years to complete.

To put that in perspective: the last time Earth was in its current position in the galaxy, dinosaurs did not yet exist - the Triassic period was just beginning. Two galactic years ago, the first multicellular animals were only just emerging.

The distance covered in a single human lifetime at galactic orbital speed is staggering. In 80 years, Earth travels roughly 571 billion kilometres - about 3,800 AU, or nearly four times the distance to the outermost edge of the Kuiper Belt. This ticker calculates exactly how far you have personally ridden on this galactic commute since your base date.

data.name: Info_GalacticCommuteSource
data.value: Data courtesy of the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Horizons On-Line Ephemeris System. Animation courtesy of European Space Agency - ESA.

data.name: Info_PhotonPathMethod
data.value:
Light leaving Earth on your base date travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second - the universal speed limit, fixed by definition since 1983. Every year that passes, that photon front expands by one light-year (about 9.46 trillion km), sweeping through an ever-growing sphere of space.

To identify which stars the light is currently passing, this ticker uses a database merging the Hipparcos, Yale Bright Star, and Gliese catalogues covering over 119,000 stars with precise parallax-based distances. A star is "reached" when its distance in light-years equals the number of years elapsed since the base date.

Some curious waypoints along the photon path:
- 4.24 ly - Proxima Centauri, our nearest stellar neighbour
- 8.6 ly - Sirius, the brightest star in Earth's night sky
- 25.1 ly - Vega, first star to have its debris disk photographed
- 640 ly - Betelgeuse, a red supergiant expected to go supernova within the next ~100,000 years

For example: if you are 40 years old, light from your birth date has already passed Sirius and dozens of other stars - and is still racing outward right now.

data.name: Info_PhotonPathSource
data.value: Star Data from the HYG Star Database (v3.0), distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 2.5 License.

data.name: Ticker_CosmicStretchFull
data.value: Since {baseDate:d}, the observable universe has expanded by approximately {distance} due to the Hubble-Lemaître law, stretching the fabric of space-time itself.

data.name: Info_CosmicStretchMethod
data.value:
The universe is not exploding into space - space itself is stretching. Every megaparsec (approximately 3.26 million light-years) of distance between two points grows by roughly 70 km/s (the Hubble constant, H₀ approx. 70 km/s/Mpc). This is not motion through space; it is the metric expansion of space-time itself, a prediction of Einstein's general relativity confirmed observationally since 1929.

The observable universe currently has a radius of approximately 46.5 billion light-years - even though the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. The difference arises because space expanded while the light was travelling. Applying H₀ to that full radius yields an overall expansion rate of roughly 3.3 million km/s for the observable boundary - greater than the speed of light, which is permitted because space itself (not matter or information) is doing the expanding.

Crucially, expansion does not affect gravitationally bound systems. The Milky Way, the Solar System, your body, and this device are all held together by forces strong enough to resist cosmic stretching. Only on scales above roughly 5 megaparsecs does expansion dominate over gravity.

This ticker calculates the incremental stretch since your base date using the current H₀ estimate (approximately 67-74 km/s/Mpc) and the scale of the observable universe, giving you a personal measure of how much the cosmos has grown in your lifetime.

data.name: Info_CosmicStretchSource
data.value:
Hubble E. "A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae" from Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 15 (3) 1929.
"The International Astronomical Union recommends that the law should now be known as the Hubble-Lemaitre law, to pay tribute to the Belgian priest and astronomer Georges Lemaitre, who derived the speed-distance relationship two years earlier than did US astronomer Edwin Hubble." from Nature 563 (7729) 2018. Animation courtesy An Atlas of The Universe, author Richard Powell.

data.name: Ticker_HumanBirthRankPostXX_Full
data.value: The moment when {baseDateName} marks the arrival of human #{estimatedRank:N0} in the story of Earth, out of all who have ever lived.

data.name: Info_HumanBirthRankMethod
data.value:
You are not just a person - you are a numbered arrival in the unbroken chain of human life. Estimating the birth rank of a person requires counting every human who ever lived before you.

Demographic historians use a combination of archaeological evidence, ancient census records, written histories, and statistical modelling to reconstruct past population curves. The scientists estimate that roughly 108 billion humans have been born since Homo sapiens emerged approximately 200,000 years ago. Of those, approximately 8.1 billion are alive today.

For births since 1900 - where reliable national-level vital statistics exist - this ticker uses a 3-epoch linear interpolation of UN and Human Mortality Database data:
• 1900-1950: roughly 50-80 million births/year, rising from post-Industrial-Revolution baselines
• 1950-2000: the Baby Boom and global development era, peaking near 140 million births/year
• 2000-present: gradual demographic transition, settling around 135 million births/year

By integrating the area under these population curves up to the specified date, the ticker derives an estimated ordinal rank - the place of somebody born on the specified date in the queue of all humans ever born. It is approximate by nature, but it is grounded in the best available science and puts your existence in a genuinely cosmic perspective.

data.name: Info_HumanBirthRankSource
data.value: World population statistics and projections courtesy of the United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (2024 Revision). Historical estimates by Human Mortality Database (2025 revision) and the Population Reference Bureau (2024).

data.name: Info_BirthRuneMethod
data.value:
Runes are among the oldest writing systems ever devised. The Elder Futhark - named for its first six letters (F-U-Þ-A-R-K) - emerged among Germanic peoples around AD 150-200, likely influenced by contact with Etruscan or Roman scripts on the Rhine and Danube frontiers. The earliest confirmed runic inscription is on the Vimose comb (Denmark, c. AD 160), reading simply "harja" - a personal name.

The 24 runes are organised into three aettir (families of eight), each associated with a Norse deity: Freyr's aett (abundance and natural forces), Hagal's aett (challenges and transformation), and Tyr's aett (order, justice, and heroism).

The birth rune system maps the solar year onto the 24-rune cycle. Each rune governs roughly 13-16 days of the year, corresponding to the Sun's progress through the sky as tracked by Norse farmers and navigators. The birth rune is therefore a snapshot of which archetypal force the Norse associated with the season of a person's arrival.

The Elder Futhark fell out of everyday use around AD 700-800, replaced by the simplified 16-rune Younger Futhark as Old Norse evolved. It survived in ritual and memorial contexts and was comprehensively decoded by 19th-century runologists, most notably Wilhelm Grimm (of fairy-tale fame).

data.name: Info_BirthRuneSource
data.value: Runic interpretations based on the Elder Futhark system of the historical Viking Age.

data.name: Ticker_PersonalYearFull_Template
data.value:
In Numerology, for those who were born on {baseDate:d}, year {curYear} is Personal Year {personalYear}:
{interpretations[personalYear - 1].Full}

data.name: PersonalYear1_Full
data.value: Personal Year 1 is characterized by feelings of loneliness and challenges in relationships, as individuals seek greater independence and pursue new beginnings. This shift can cause tension with partners used to doing things together, leading to misunderstandings. People often do not realize their desire for solitude is influenced by this year's vibration, making it hard to explain their actions. The experience varies - some may face situations requiring assertiveness, and failing to seize these opportunities can result in loss or loneliness. Despite the challenges, Personal Year 1 offers a chance for renewal, rest from past responsibilities, and rewards for previous efforts. While important connections may be formed, romantic relationships typically begin in Personal Years 2 or 6.

data.name: PersonalYear2_Full
data.value: Personal Year 2 is a time for forming new relationships, increased cooperation, and sharing emotions. People become more understanding and prefer connecting with others rather than being alone. Ideas and opportunities from the previous year can now grow, and maintaining a peaceful environment is important to avoid stress and illness. Overall, it is a period of harmony, support, and personal growth.

data.name: PersonalYear3_Full
data.value: The vibrations of the number three encourage mental activity, social interaction, and self-expression. This year is not suited for routine tasks; instead, it demands stimulating and imaginative pursuits to channel increased mental energy. If not properly directed, this energy can lead to irritability or sleep disturbances. The period also brings opportunities to resolve past relationships and issues, often through rational communication, which helps alleviate emotional distress. Additionally, it is an ideal time for studying, as mental energy reaches its peak.

data.name: PersonalYear4_Full
data.value: Personal Year 4 is an active period requiring efficient energy management. People are prone to overwork, ignoring warning signs, and making impulsive decisions that can lead to setbacks. Challenges often arise, making security and future planning a priority; many prefer staying home and focusing on family. This year favors property purchases and investments, but individuals may seek support due to self-doubt and difficulty recognizing their progress. Effective organization and stress management are crucial to avoid health issues. By channeling energy constructively and learning to relax, Personal Year 4 can yield significant success.

data.name: Info_PersonalYearMethod
data.value:
Numbers have fascinated humanity for as long as we have counted. Long before the word "numerology" existed, the practice was called arithmancy (from Greek arithmos = number, manteia = divination) - the art of drawing meaning from numerical relationships.

The earliest systematic number mysticism appears in Pythagorean philosophy (6th century BC). Pythagoras taught that numbers were the fundamental reality underlying all phenomena - odd numbers were masculine and active, even numbers feminine and passive, and the number 10 (the tetractys) was sacred. His school in Croton, southern Italy, treated mathematics as a spiritual discipline.

Parallel traditions developed independently: Gematria in Jewish Kabbalah assigned numerical values to Hebrew letters to find hidden meanings in scripture; Isopsephy did the same in ancient Greek; the I Ching in China built a 64-symbol divination system on binary-like number patterns.

The Personal Year calculation used here follows the Pythagorean system: add the digits of your birth month and day to the digits of the current calendar year, then reduce to a single digit (1-9). This number describes the dominant energetic theme of your year - a 9-year cycle of growth, consolidation, and renewal that repeats throughout your life.

data.name: Info_PersonalYearSource
data.value: Personal Year calculations based on the Pythagorean system of Numerology.

data.value: The universe has been busy! Approximately {stars_born} stars have ignited and {supernovas} supernovae have flared since this date.

data.name: Info_VibrantCosmosMethod
data.value:
The universe is a perpetual stellar factory. At any given moment, clouds of hydrogen and helium are collapsing under gravity across billions of galaxies, igniting new stars - while the most massive ones are ending their lives in cataclysmic supernova explosions.

Star formation rate: The current observations estimate the present-day universe births approximately 4,800 stars per second across all observable galaxies. This rate was much higher 10 billion years ago - the "cosmic noon" era of peak star formation - and has been declining ever since as available gas is consumed.

Supernova rate: Massive stars (above roughly 8 solar masses) live fast and die explosively. The scientists estimate approximately 30 core-collapse supernovae per second across the observable universe (particularly, supernovae occur in the Milky Way approximately once every 40 to 50 years). A single supernova briefly outshines its entire host galaxy and seeds the surrounding space with heavy elements - the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were forged in supernovas that preceded our Solar System.

These rates are averages across the roughly 2 trillion galaxies in the observable universe. Even at the current "quiet" modern rate, the numbers accumulated over a human lifetime are genuinely astronomical.

data.name: Info_VibrantCosmosSource
data.value: Star Formation Rate (SFR) sourced from the NASA/ESA Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) and findings from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) deep field surveys. Supernova Frequency estimates from the International Astronomical Union (IAU).

data.name: Ticker_CellularRefreshFull
data.value: Your body has completely replaced its outer skin layer {skin_count} times and generated roughly {rbc_count_billions} {unit_billion} RBCs new red blood cells since {baseDate:d}.

data.name: Info_CellularRefreshMethod
data.value:
You are not the same physical body you were a decade ago - almost every cell in you has been replaced. The human body maintains itself through continuous cell mitosis, a process of division and renewal that varies dramatically by tissue type.

Skin (epidermis): The outermost layer renews approximately every 27 days. Dead keratinocytes are shed continuously - roughly 30,000-40,000 cells per hour - and replaced from the basal layer below. In a 70-year lifetime, you shed and regrow your skin surface about 900 times.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes): RBCs make up approximately 70% of all human cells by count. They have no nucleus and cannot divide, so the body manufactures approximately 2 million new RBCs every second in the bone marrow - a process called erythropoiesis. Each RBC lives for roughly 120 days before being recycled by the spleen. In a single day your body produces and retires about 173 billion of them.

The total number of RBCs in the average adult body at any moment is approximately 25 trillion. Still, the cumulative production since your birth - shown by this ticker if to set your birth date as the base date - dwarfs even that staggering standing inventory.

data.name: Info_CellularRefreshSource
data.value: Calculation based on the data provided by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) of the National Library of Medicine (NIH). Animation based on images in Wikimedia Commons, author Roy van Heesbeen.

data.name: Info_YourBreathMethod
data.value:
Every breath you take is a chemical transaction with the planet. You inhale oxygen produced by photosynthesis and exhale CO₂ that plants, oceans, and soils will absorb - you are a node in the global carbon cycle.

The calculation uses currently accepted physiological averages:
• Breathing rate: 12-16 breaths/min at rest; this ticker uses the midpoint of 14 breaths/min
• Tidal volume: approximately 0.5 litres of air per breath
• CO₂ per day: combined with tidal volume and breath rate this yields approximately 1.04 kg of CO₂ per day

Over 80 years, a single human exhales approximately 30,000 kg of CO₂ - about the mass of 3 average passenger cars. Biological respiration is part of a closed loop: every molecule you exhale was recently fixed from the atmosphere by a plant or alga.

This ticker makes that invisible, lifelong metabolic footprint visible - breath by breath.

data.value: Calculation based on the data provided by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) of the National Library of Medicine (NIH). Images courtesy of SVG Repo LLC, FreePNGimg, Share Icon, UXWing.

data.name: Info_GlobalExhaleMethod
data.value:
Since the Industrial Revolution, humanity has been running a one-way carbon experiment on a planetary scale. The Global Carbon Project tracks CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels, cement production, and land-use change every year.

Key milestones in the data:
• Pre-1900: Cumulative industrial emissions were under 50 Gt CO₂ - a rounding error in geological terms
• 1950: The "Great Acceleration" began; annual emissions roughly doubled every 25 years
• 1990: The first IPCC assessment; global emissions were roughly 22 Gt/year
• 2023: Record high of roughly 36.8 Gt CO₂ from fossil fuels alone (Global Carbon Budget 2023)

The concentration of CO₂ in the atmosphere has risen from roughly 280 ppm pre-industrially to over 422 ppm as of 2024 - the highest level in at least 3 million years.

This ticker calculates cumulative emissions since the specified date by interpolating against the GCP's annual time series. The goal is to make an abstract global statistic personally tangible.

data.name: Info_GlobalExhaleSource
data.value: Emissions data courtesy of the Global Carbon Project (GCP) and the Global Carbon Budget (GCB) of University of Exeter's Global Systems Institute.

data.name: Info_GlobalCrowdMethod
data.value:
Seven billion. Eight billion. Each headline number obscures the relentless, second-by-second churn underneath: roughly 4.4 babies born and 2.0 people dying every second, yielding a net gain of approximately 2.35 humans per second - or about 74 million more people each year.

This ticker models population growth using a 3-epoch linear approximation calibrated against the today's approximation data:
• Pre-1950: global population rose from roughly 1.6 billion (1900) to 2.5 billion (1950), averaging about 18 million net additions per year
• 1950-2000: the demographic explosion driven by post-war medicine and the Green Revolution; net additions peaked at roughly 90 million/year in the late 1980s
• 2000-present: growth continues but decelerates as fertility rates fall in developing regions; current net additions are approximately 80 million/year and declining

The model distributes the annual net change uniformly across seconds within each epoch.

The result: a live estimate of how many more people share the planet with you compared to when your timeline began.

data.value:
Since {baseDateName} on {baseDate:d}, an average person would have spent their time on:
{all_activities_list}

data.name: Info_LifeLogMethod
data.value:
Time is the one resource that cannot be replenished - yet most of us have only a vague intuition of how we spend it. This ticker makes the invisible ledger concrete.

The calculation is straightforward: total days elapsed x average daily hours per activity.

Some findings that consistently surprise people:
• The average adult spends roughly 9 hours a day sleeping and in personal care combined - more time than most paid jobs
• Leisure and screen time averages roughly 5 hours/day, meaning a 40-year-old has spent roughly 8 years watching screens
• Eating and drinking takes roughly 1.2 hours/day; over a lifetime of 80 years that accumulates to nearly 4 years
• The average commuter spends roughly 27 minutes each way, adding up to nearly a full year of travel by retirement

These are population averages, not prescriptions. But seeing the cumulative totals - rendered in years rather than minutes per day - tends to prompt a genuine recalibration of what we consider "how we spend our time."

data.name: Info_LifeLogSource
data.value: Averages based on time-tracking statistics from the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and comparable OECD international surveys.

data.name: Ticker_SpaceWaitFull
data.value: Your next extraterrestrial milestone is your {age} birthday on {planet}! It happens in exactly {countdown} on {nextDate}.

data.name: Info_SpaceWaitMethod
data.value:
A planetary year is defined by one thing only: how long a body takes to complete one full orbit around the Sun. That period is set by orbital mechanics - specifically, the balance between the Sun's gravitational pull and the planet's orbital speed - and varies from 88 Earth days (Mercury) to 165 Earth years (Neptune) and even more for bodies in the Oort cloud.

This ticker takes the passed period in Earth days and divides it by each planet's orbital period to compute the next "anniversary" on every world. It then identifies the one arriving soonest - and counts down to it.

Orbital periods used:
• Mercury: 87.97 Earth days
• Venus: 224.70 Earth days
• Mars: 686.97 Earth days (roughly 1.88 years)
• Jupiter: 4,332.59 Earth days (roughly 11.86 years)
• Saturn: 10,759.22 Earth days (roughly 29.46 years)
• Uranus: 30,688.50 Earth days (roughly 84 years)
• Neptune: 60,195.00 Earth days (roughly 165 years; no chances to be chosen for dates since the year 1900)

Thus, on Mercury, you celebrate a birthday every 3 months - a 30-year-old has had over 120 Mercurian birthdays. On Neptune, no human alive may complete a single orbit: since the planet was discovered in 1846, it finished its first observed full orbit only in 2011.

data.name: Info_SpaceWaitSource
data.value: Orbital periods (in Earth days) sourced from the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Planetary Fact Sheet.

data.comment: CalculationService.cs - HTML-formattable full text; all tokens replaced with N0 values

data.name: Info_VibrantHumanityMethod
data.value:
Every second, the human family changes. Globally, roughly 4.4 babies are born and 2.0 people die every second, producing a continuous net gain of around 2.4 lives per second - a churn of staggering scale when accumulated over years or decades.

To model this accurately across history, the ticker uses a 3-epoch linear approximation:
• 1900-1950: slower growth era; global births roughly 50-80 million/year, deaths close behind
• 1950-2000: the demographic explosion - post-war medicine, falling infant mortality, and the Green Revolution drove births to peak near 140 million/year
• 2000-present: fertility decline in developed and developing regions alike; net growth decelerating but still ~80 million/year

The sub-statistics are derived from validated fixed global ratios:
• Twins: approximately 2.4% of all births - a rate that has risen sharply since the 1980s due to IVF and older maternal age
• Heart disease and stroke: approximately 27% of all deaths - the single largest cause of mortality worldwide since 1990
• Cancer: approximately 18% of all deaths - second largest cause, with incidence rising as populations age and survive infectious disease

A striking perspective: of all humans who have ever lived (estimated at roughly 108 billion by the PRB), more than 7% are alive right now - an unusually high share driven by the population surge of the last century.

data.name: Info_VibrantHumanitySource
data.value: World population statistics and projections courtesy of the United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (2024 Revision). Historical estimates by Human Mortality Database (2025 revision) and the Population Reference Bureau (2024). Sub-statistics (twins and causes of death) are derived using fixed global ratios provided by the WHO Global Health Estimates and demographic researches.

data.name: Info_VibrantNatureMethod
data.value:
Taxonomy (the describing of new species) has accelerated due to better technology, more scientists, and genetic sequencing.

• 1900-1950: The rate was relatively steady, relying on traditional field biology. Scientists described roughly 10,000 species per year (approx. 27.4 per day).
• 1950-2000: Post-WWII scientific expansion and global travel increased the rate to roughly 15,000 species per year (approx. 41.1 per day).
• 2000-Present: With the advent of DNA barcoding and deep-sea/canopy exploration, the International Institute for Species Exploration (IISE) notes we describe about 18,000 species per year (approx. 49.3 per day).

Estimating extinctions is harder because we cannot easily measure what we have not discovered, but conservation organizations (like the UN IPBES and WWF) track the background rate versus the modern Holocene extinction rate.

• 1900-1950: Industrialization expanded, but massive global habitat loss was just beginning. A conservative estimate for this era is approx. 10 species lost per day.
• 1950-2000: The Great Acceleration of human population, agriculture, and climate change. The estimated loss rose significantly to approx. 50 species per day.
• 2000-Present: Current UN estimates suggest dozens to over a hundred species go extinct daily. Using a conservative but impactful scientific consensus, we can approximate approx. 150 species lost per day in the modern era.

The taxonomic breakdowns apply robust historical proportions from the Catalogue of Life and IUCN:
• Insects/Invertebrates make up approximately 55% of discoveries and approximately 60% of total extinction volume,
• Plants make up approximately 15% of discoveries,
• Vertebrates (mammals, birds, fish, etc.) make up roughly 2% of both.

data.name: Info_VibrantNatureSource
data.value: Approximations derived from the International Institute for Species Exploration (IISE), the Catalogue of Life taxonomic distribution, and extinction rate estimates from the UN Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES). Image designed by Freepik.
